props.title: Blue Collar
props.initialSlug: Three autoworkers clash with union and mob power

sections.content: Paul Schrader's directorial debut Blue Collar (1978) hits like a sledgehammer, capturing working-class desperation through three auto workers played by Richard Pryor, Harvey Keitel, and Yaphet Kotto. The film brutally depicts labor exploitation at a Detroit auto plant, showing how corporate and union corruption crush worker solidarity. It shares DNA with other gritty 70s workplace dramas like F.I.S.T. (1978) and Norma Rae (1979), but Blue Collar's unflinching examination of how capitalism pits workers against each other feels more relevant than ever.

sections.content: The film's influence echoes through later working-class narratives like Gung Ho (1986) and American Factory (2019), but few match its savage critique of how management weaponizes racial tensions to prevent unified labor action. Schrader and co-writer Leonard Schrader drew from real Detroit auto plant conditions, creating a docudrama feel similar to The Killing Floor (1984) about Chicago meatpackers. The film's mix of workplace realism and crime thriller elements influenced later films like Out of the Furnace (2013).

What sets Blue Collar apart is Richard Pryor's devastating dramatic performance, proving his range far beyond comedy. The film's unforgettable factory sequences, shot in a real auto plant, capture industrial work's grinding toll with documentary-like precision. This attention to workplace authenticity influenced films like Silkwood (1983) and North Country (2005), though few match Blue Collar's raw intensity. SUBHEAD: Labor Movement on Film

sections.content: Blue Collar kicked off a vital cycle of late 70s labor films including Norma Rae (1979) and 9 to 5 (1980), reflecting widespread union activism of the era. Its influence extends to contemporary workplace dramas like Support the Girls (2018) and Sorry We Missed You (2019), though modern films often focus more on service industry exploitation than traditional manufacturing. The film's themes of worker solidarity being undermined by management manipulation remain painfully relevant.
